lessons.title: Context, Allegory & Orwell's Purpose
lessons.description: Why Orwell wrote Animal Farm and how it mirrors the Russian Revolution and Stalin's rise.
lessons.content_html:
Why Did Orwell Write Animal Farm?

George Orwell published Animal Farm in 1945, at a time when the Soviet Union was Britain’s wartime ally. Despite this, Orwell was deeply critical of communism as practised under Joseph Stalin. He had witnessed authoritarian behaviour first-hand while fighting in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), where Soviet-backed communists betrayed and purged their own allies.

Key Fact

Orwell described Animal Farm as the first book in which he tried “to fuse political purpose and artistic purpose into one whole.”

Orwell was a democratic socialist — he supported equality but opposed dictatorships of any kind. He saw how Stalin had corrupted the original ideals of the 1917 Russian Revolution, turning a movement for workers’ liberation into a brutal regime. Animal Farm was his way of warning readers that revolutions can be hijacked by the very people they were meant to overthrow.

What Is an Allegory?

An allegory is a story that works on two levels: the surface narrative (animals running a farm) and a hidden meaning (the Russian Revolution and its aftermath). Every major character and event in Animal Farm maps onto a real historical figure or moment.

Old Major = Karl Marx / Vladimir Lenin — the visionary who inspires revolution but dies before it is corrupted.

Napoleon = Joseph Stalin — the cunning leader who seizes power through force, propaganda, and fear.

Snowball = Leon Trotsky — the intellectual rival who is expelled and then blamed for everything.

Squealer = Soviet propaganda machine (Pravda newspaper) — manipulates language to justify the pigs’ actions.

Boxer = The loyal working class — exploited until no longer useful, then discarded.

Mr Jones = Tsar Nicholas II — the incompetent ruler overthrown by revolution.

The Russian Revolution — Essential Context

In 1917, the Russian people overthrew Tsar Nicholas II, who had ruled as an autocrat while millions starved. The Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, promised “Peace, Land, Bread” — equality for all workers. After Lenin’s death in 1924, a power struggle erupted between Stalin and Trotsky. Stalin won, exiled Trotsky, and established a totalitarian dictatorship.

Key Fact

Stalin’s regime killed millions through forced collectivisation, purges, and famine. Orwell wrote Animal Farm to expose how “All animals are equal” becomes “but some animals are more equal than others.”

Orwell had several interlinked purposes:

1. To warn against totalitarianism: Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. The pigs begin as liberators and end as tyrants indistinguishable from humans.

2. To show how propaganda enables dictatorship: Squealer’s manipulation of language — rewriting the commandments, distorting the truth — shows that controlling language means controlling thought.

3. To criticise the complacency of the masses: The animals’ failure to question authority allows the pigs to seize power unchecked. Orwell suggests ordinary people must stay vigilant.

4. To satirise the Soviet Union specifically: The book is a direct attack on Stalinist Russia, showing how revolutionary ideals were betrayed step by step.

The Genre: Fable and Satire

Animal Farm is both a fable and a satire. As a fable, it uses animals to deliver a moral message. As a satire, it uses irony and dark humour to expose the absurdity and cruelty of totalitarian rule. The simple, fairy-tale style makes the political message accessible — Orwell called it “a fairy story” in its subtitle, which is itself ironic given the violence and betrayal within.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the AQA exam, you will answer on Animal Farm in Section B of Paper 2 (Modern Texts). You will be given an extract and asked to write about the extract and the whole novel. Always link Orwell’s methods to his purpose — examiners reward answers that explain why Orwell made particular choices, not just what happens. Use the phrase “Orwell uses [technique] to [effect] in order to [purpose]” as a structural frame.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Orwell wrote Animal Farm to expose how Stalin betrayed the ideals of the Russian Revolution and to warn against totalitarianism.
  • The novella is an allegory — every character and event maps onto a real historical figure or moment.
  • Understanding Orwell’s context and purpose is essential for achieving top marks in the exam.

lessons.title: Old Major's Speech & the Rebellion
lessons.description: How Old Major's rhetoric inspires revolution and what Orwell reveals about idealism and power.
lessons.content_html:
Old Major’s Speech (Chapter 1)

The novella opens with Old Major, the prize-winning boar, calling a meeting in the barn. He delivers a passionate speech arguing that Man is the enemy of all animals. He tells them that their lives are “miserable, laborious, and short” because humans exploit their labour and give nothing in return. This speech is the catalyst for the revolution that follows.

Key Fact

Old Major represents Karl Marx (who developed communist theory) and Vladimir Lenin (who led the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution). Like Marx, Old Major dies before his ideas are put into practice — and like Lenin, his vision is later corrupted.

Orwell’s Use of Rhetoric

Old Major’s speech is a masterclass in rhetoric. Orwell deliberately crafts it to sound inspiring and logical, showing readers how revolutionary leaders use language to mobilise support.

Inclusive pronouns: “We are born, we are given just so much food…” — Old Major uses “we” to unite the animals and create a sense of shared suffering.

Rhetorical questions: “Is it not crystal clear, comrades?” — forces the audience to agree without questioning the logic.

Repetition: The repeated address “comrades” builds solidarity and a sense of collective identity.

Emotive language: Words like “miserable,” “slavery,” and “cruelty” provoke anger and resentment toward humans.

Rule of three: “No animal in England knows the meaning of happiness or leisure or retirement” — hammers home the point.

Old Major also teaches the animals the song “Beasts of England,” which functions as a revolutionary anthem. The song imagines a future utopia free from human tyranny: “Rings shall vanish from our noses, / And the harness from our back.” It gives the animals a shared vision and emotional fuel for rebellion.

The Rebellion (Chapter 2)

Three nights after his speech, Old Major dies peacefully in his sleep. Over the following months, the pigs — recognised as the cleverest animals — develop his ideas into a complete system of thought called Animalism. Napoleon, Snowball, and Squealer take the lead in spreading these ideas.

Key Fact

The Rebellion happens spontaneously when Mr Jones forgets to feed the animals. Orwell shows that revolutions are often triggered by immediate suffering (hunger) rather than ideology alone — mirroring how the Russian people revolted partly due to bread shortages.

The animals drive Jones and his men off the farm. They rename it “Animal Farm” and paint the Seven Commandments on the barn wall. The most important commandment is: “All animals are equal.” The early days feel hopeful — the animals work together, the harvest is a success, and there is a genuine sense of freedom.

The Seven Commandments include rules like “No animal shall sleep in a bed,” “No animal shall drink alcohol,” and “No animal shall kill any other animal.” These rules are presented as unbreakable principles, but Orwell plants the seeds of their corruption from the start.

Notice that it is the pigs who write the commandments. The other animals cannot read well enough to check them. This literacy gap is crucial — Orwell shows that control of knowledge is control of power. Those who cannot read the rules cannot hold their leaders accountable.

Also notice the detail that the pigs keep the milk and apples for themselves almost immediately. Squealer justifies this with the argument that pigs need brain food to manage the farm. This is the first sign that “equality” is already being undermined.

Orwell’s Purpose in Chapters 1–2

Orwell structures the opening to create dramatic irony. Readers familiar with history know the revolution will be betrayed, so the animals’ optimism becomes poignant and tragic. By making Old Major’s ideals genuinely appealing, Orwell ensures readers understand that the tragedy lies not in the revolution itself, but in its corruption by those who seize power.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing Old Major’s speech, always connect the rhetorical technique to Orwell’s wider purpose. For example: “Orwell uses inclusive pronouns in Old Major’s speech to show how revolutionary leaders unite people through shared grievance — but this unity is later exploited by Napoleon, suggesting Orwell warns that collective emotion can be manipulated.” This approach links AO2 (methods) to AO3 (context) seamlessly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Old Major’s speech uses rhetorical techniques (inclusive pronouns, repetition, emotive language) to inspire revolution — Orwell shows how language is a tool of power.
  • The Rebellion succeeds because of immediate suffering (hunger), not just ideology — mirroring the Russian Revolution.
  • The pigs’ early seizure of milk and apples foreshadows the corruption of Animalism’s ideals.

lessons.title: The Early Farm & Squealer's Propaganda
lessons.description: How the pigs consolidate power through propaganda, manipulation of language, and control of knowledge.
lessons.content_html:
The Early Days of Animal Farm

After the Rebellion, life on the farm seems genuinely better. The animals work hard, the harvest is successful, and there is a sense of pride and community. Orwell describes this period in positive, almost utopian terms — the animals feel “happy as they had never conceived it possible to be.” Every mouthful of food was “an acute positive pleasure” because it was truly their own.

However, Orwell plants the seeds of future corruption immediately. The pigs do not do any physical labour — instead, they supervise and direct the other animals. This division between mental and physical labour mirrors the class divisions that the revolution was supposed to eliminate. The pigs also teach themselves to read and write from an old spelling book, giving them exclusive access to knowledge.

Key Fact

Orwell shows that the new hierarchy forms almost immediately. The pigs position themselves as the “brain workers” of the farm, exploiting the other animals’ inability to read. This mirrors how the Soviet elite (the nomenklatura) lived in privilege while claiming to represent the workers.

Squealer — The Voice of Propaganda

Propaganda is one of the most important themes in Animal Farm, and Squealer is its embodiment. He is described as a small, fat pig with “very round cheeks, twinkling eyes, nimble movements, and a shrill voice.” Most importantly, Orwell tells us he could “turn black into white” — meaning he can make any argument sound convincing, no matter how dishonest.

Fear: Squealer repeatedly asks, “Surely, comrades, you do not want Jones to come back?” This creates a false dilemma — either accept the pigs’ rule or suffer under Jones. There is no middle option.

Pseudo-science: He uses invented statistics and claims backed by no evidence: “It has been proved by science, comrades, that a pig’s metabolism requires apples and milk.”

Rhetorical questions: These force the animals to agree without thinking: “Surely there is no one among you who wants to see Jones come back?”

Rewriting history: As the novella progresses, Squealer gradually alters the Seven Commandments and rewrites the history of the Rebellion to suit Napoleon’s narrative.

The Milk and Apples Incident

The first concrete example of inequality comes when the pigs claim all the milk and windfall apples for themselves. When the animals question this, Squealer delivers his first major propaganda speech. He argues that pigs need these foods because they are “brain workers” and that the farm’s entire management depends on them. He finishes with the threat: “Do you know what would happen if we pigs failed in our duty? Jones would come back!”

Key Fact

Orwell reveals that the other animals find Squealer’s argument unanswerable — not because it is logical, but because they cannot articulate a counter-argument and are afraid of Jones’s return. This shows how propaganda works: it exploits fear and intellectual inequality.

Orwell shows several reasons why the animals accept the pigs’ growing power:

Illiteracy: Most animals cannot read beyond a few letters, so they cannot check the commandments or challenge Squealer’s claims.

Trust: The animals trust the pigs because they led the revolution. They assume the pigs are acting in everyone’s interest.

Fear: The threat of Jones’s return is powerful enough to silence dissent.

Simplicity: Boxer’s maxim, “Napoleon is always right,” shows how blind loyalty replaces critical thinking.

Orwell’s Message About Language and Power

Through Squealer, Orwell argues that language is the most powerful tool of oppression. Those who control the narrative control the people. Squealer does not use physical force — he uses words to reshape reality. This reflects Orwell’s lifelong concern about political language, which he explored further in his essay “Politics and the English Language” (1946) and his later novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Squealer, always identify the specific technique (e.g. rhetorical question, false dilemma, appeal to fear) and explain its effect on the animals and its wider significance for Orwell’s message. Examiners at the top level want to see you connect language analysis (AO2) to purpose and context (AO3) in every paragraph.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The pigs immediately establish themselves as a privileged class through their literacy and role as “brain workers.”
  • Squealer uses propaganda techniques — fear, pseudo-science, rhetorical questions, and historical revisionism — to justify inequality.
  • Orwell’s central argument is that controlling language means controlling thought — propaganda enables tyranny.

lessons.title: The Battle of the Cowshed & Snowball's Leadership
lessons.description: How Snowball's bravery and ideas contrast with Napoleon's scheming, and why history is rewritten.
lessons.content_html:
Snowball’s Character and Leadership

Snowball is presented as the intellectual, idealistic pig who genuinely tries to improve life for all animals. He organises committees to teach the animals to read, plans improvements to the farm, and studies military strategy from a book about Julius Caesar’s campaigns. He represents Leon Trotsky — the brilliant but ultimately outmanoeuvred rival to Stalin.

Key Fact

Orwell presents Snowball as “quicker in speech and more inventive” than Napoleon, but “not considered to have the same depth of character.” This contrast is crucial: Napoleon is less intelligent but more ruthless — and in the power struggle, ruthlessness wins.

Snowball’s committees include an Egg Production Committee, a Clean Tails League, and literacy classes. While most fail, they show genuine effort to include all animals in the revolution’s benefits. His motto is “Four legs good, two legs bad” — a simplification of Animalism designed for the less intelligent animals, especially the sheep.

The Battle of the Cowshed (Chapter 4)

In October, Jones and a group of men from neighbouring farms attempt to retake Animal Farm. Snowball has anticipated this and prepared a defensive strategy. He leads the animals bravely, charging directly at Jones and receiving a wound from his shotgun. The animals win a decisive victory, and Snowball is hailed as a hero.

Snowball organises a two-phase strategy: a feigned retreat to lure the men into the yard, followed by an ambush from three sides. This shows his tactical intelligence — he has studied military history and applies it effectively.

Snowball is awarded “Animal Hero, First Class” for his bravery. A decoration that Napoleon will later claim for himself.

Boxer also fights heroically, knocking a stable boy unconscious with his hoof. He is distressed, thinking he has killed the boy — showing his gentle nature despite his enormous strength.

The battle allegorically represents the Russian Civil War (1918–1922), when the Bolsheviks fought off counter-revolutionary forces supported by foreign powers.

Napoleon vs. Snowball — The Growing Rivalry

From the start, Napoleon and Snowball disagree on almost everything. Snowball wants to spread the revolution to other farms; Napoleon focuses on consolidating power at home. Snowball draws up plans for a windmill that would bring electricity and reduce the animals’ workload to three days a week. Napoleon opposes the windmill — or rather, he opposes Snowball having the credit for it.

Key Fact

The windmill debate represents the historical conflict between Trotsky (who advocated for rapid industrialisation and spreading revolution internationally) and Stalin (who promoted “socialism in one country” and consolidated domestic power). Napoleon’s rejection of the windmill mirrors Stalin’s initial opposition to Trotsky’s policies — though he later adopts them as his own.

After Snowball’s expulsion (which happens in the next chapter), Squealer gradually rewrites the history of the Battle of the Cowshed. He claims that Snowball was actually a coward and a traitor who fought alongside Jones. Napoleon, Squealer claims, was the true hero of the battle — despite having been barely mentioned during it.

This historical revisionism mirrors Stalin’s treatment of Trotsky: after exiling him in 1929, Stalin had Trotsky airbrushed out of photographs and rewritten out of Soviet history books. Orwell shows that controlling the past is essential to controlling the present.

The animals gradually accept the new version of events because they cannot remember the details clearly, and Squealer’s confident delivery makes them doubt their own memories. Orwell suggests that without records and literacy, truth becomes whatever the powerful say it is.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing Snowball and Napoleon, focus on Orwell’s structural choices. Snowball is given speeches, plans, and heroic actions, while Napoleon operates through silence, secrecy, and proxies (Squealer, the dogs). This contrast in characterisation methods is itself Orwell’s comment on how democratic and authoritarian leaders operate differently. Making this point earns high AO2 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Snowball represents Trotsky — an intellectual idealist outmanoeuvred by Napoleon’s ruthlessness.
  • The Battle of the Cowshed shows Snowball’s genuine heroism, which is later erased through historical revisionism.
  • Orwell uses the rewriting of the battle’s history to show how totalitarian regimes control the narrative by controlling the past.

lessons.title: Napoleon's Rise to Power
lessons.description: How Napoleon uses the dogs, fear, and Snowball's expulsion to seize absolute control of the farm.
lessons.content_html:
The Expulsion of Snowball (Chapter 5)

The pivotal moment in Animal Farm comes when Napoleon uses his secretly trained dogs to chase Snowball off the farm. During a debate about the windmill, Snowball delivers an eloquent speech that is winning the animals over. Napoleon responds not with argument but with force — he gives a “high-pitched whimper” and nine enormous dogs burst into the barn, chasing Snowball through a gap in the hedge. He is never seen again.

Key Fact

Napoleon had secretly taken nine puppies from their mothers early in the novella, claiming he would “educate” them. They reappear as his personal attack force — representing Stalin’s secret police (the NKVD/KGB). Orwell shows that Napoleon planned this coup from the very beginning.

This moment transforms the farm from a flawed democracy into a dictatorship. Napoleon immediately abolishes the Sunday meetings where animals could debate and vote. Instead, a committee of pigs will make all decisions privately. The animals are stunned but cannot resist — the dogs growl at anyone who starts to protest.

How Napoleon Consolidates Power

After expelling Snowball, Napoleon uses several strategies to cement his authority. Each mirrors a technique used by real-world dictators, particularly Stalin.

1. Military force (the dogs): The dogs act as Napoleon’s bodyguards and enforcers. They surround him, growl at dissenters, and later participate in the purges. They represent the secret police who maintained Stalin’s power through fear and violence.

2. Propaganda (Squealer): After every controversial decision, Squealer explains why it was necessary. He rewrites history, fabricates statistics, and uses the constant threat of Jones’s return to justify Napoleon’s actions.

3. Scapegoating Snowball: Napoleon blames Snowball for everything that goes wrong. When the windmill collapses, it is “Snowball’s sabotage.” When crops fail, Snowball is the cause. This gives the animals an external enemy to fear, diverting attention from Napoleon’s failings.

4. Controlling information: With Snowball gone and the Sunday debates abolished, Napoleon controls all communication. The animals receive information only through Squealer, and they cannot verify anything independently.

Key Fact

Orwell shows that Napoleon never gives a single public speech after seizing power. All communication goes through Squealer. This intermediary system prevents direct accountability — Napoleon can deny anything Squealer says if it proves unpopular.

The Windmill — Napoleon’s Hypocrisy

Three weeks after expelling Snowball for proposing the windmill, Napoleon announces that the windmill will be built after all. Squealer explains that Napoleon had never actually opposed the windmill — his apparent opposition was a “manoeuvre” to get rid of Snowball, who was “a dangerous character and a bad influence.” This hypocrisy is breathtaking, yet the animals accept it.

Boxer is confused by Napoleon’s reversal on the windmill. He tries to think it through but ultimately falls back on his personal motto: “Napoleon is always right.” This is one of the novella’s most powerful and tragic moments.

Boxer represents the decent, hardworking majority who are exploited by authoritarian leaders. His loyalty is genuine but unthinking — and Orwell shows that such blind loyalty is exactly what dictators need to stay in power. Boxer’s strength could overthrow Napoleon, but his trust prevents him from ever using it.

The contrast between Boxer and Benjamin the donkey is also significant. Benjamin is intelligent enough to see through the pigs’ lies, but his cynical passivity (“Donkeys live a long time”) makes him equally complicit. Orwell criticises both blind loyalty and intellectual apathy.

Orwell’s Warning

Chapter 5 is the turning point of the novella. Orwell shows that the transition from democracy to dictatorship can happen in a single moment — the coup is swift, violent, and irreversible. Once the dogs enforce Napoleon’s will, there is no mechanism for the animals to remove him. Orwell’s warning is clear: democratic institutions must be protected, because once they are destroyed, they are almost impossible to restore.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Chapter 5 is a rich source for extract-based questions. If the extract comes from this chapter, focus on the structural turning point — how the text shifts from debate to violence, from democracy to dictatorship, in a single moment. Link this to Orwell’s purpose: he shows that coups happen not through grand battles but through the sudden application of force against an unprepared population.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Napoleon uses the dogs (secret police), Squealer (propaganda), and the scapegoating of Snowball to seize and maintain absolute power.
  • The expulsion of Snowball marks the shift from democracy to dictatorship — Napoleon abolishes debate and rules by decree.
  • Boxer’s blind loyalty and Benjamin’s cynical passivity both enable Napoleon’s tyranny — Orwell warns against both.

lessons.title: The Windmill & Boxer's Exploitation
lessons.description: How the windmill symbolises false progress and how Boxer's labour is exploited by Napoleon's regime.
lessons.content_html:
Building the Windmill

After claiming Snowball’s windmill plans as his own, Napoleon forces the animals to begin construction. The work is gruelling — the animals must drag massive boulders up the quarry slope, breaking them into smaller pieces. The physical labour falls hardest on Boxer, who takes on extra shifts and adopts the motto “I will work harder.”

Key Fact

The windmill symbolises Stalin’s Five-Year Plans — ambitious industrialisation projects that promised modernisation but were built on the suffering of ordinary workers. Like the Five-Year Plans, the windmill is repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, consuming enormous effort for little benefit to the working animals.

Meanwhile, the pigs do no physical labour at all. They “supervised and directed” from a distance. The gap between the ruling class (pigs) and the working class (other animals) grows ever wider, yet Squealer assures everyone that the pigs’ mental work is the most important contribution to the farm.

The Windmill Falls

In November, a violent storm destroys the half-built windmill. Napoleon immediately blames sabotage by Snowball, declaring “Snowball has done this thing!” He sentences Snowball to death in absentia and orders the animals to begin rebuilding immediately, despite the approaching winter.

Blaming Snowball serves multiple purposes for Napoleon:

Deflects blame: The real cause of the collapse is poor construction — the walls were too thin. By blaming Snowball, Napoleon avoids accountability for his own failures.

Maintains an external enemy: Every totalitarian regime needs an enemy to unite people against. Snowball becomes Animal Farm’s permanent scapegoat.

Justifies increased control: The “threat” of Snowball allows Napoleon to demand greater sacrifices from the animals and punish anyone who questions him as a “Snowball agent.”

Boxer — The Tragic Hero

Boxer is the emotional heart of the novella. He is enormously strong, utterly loyal, and completely trusting. His two slogans — “I will work harder” and “Napoleon is always right” — define his character: he responds to every problem with more effort and more obedience, never with questioning or resistance.

Key Fact

Orwell uses Boxer to represent the proletariat — the working class whose labour sustains the regime but who receive nothing in return. Boxer’s tragedy is that his strength could overthrow Napoleon, but his trust prevents him from ever using it against the pigs.

Boxer wakes an hour before everyone else to work on the windmill. He volunteers for every difficult task. When food rations are reduced, he works even harder. When Squealer distorts history, Boxer accepts it because he trusts Napoleon.

The other animals admire Boxer and take inspiration from his work ethic, but Orwell presents this admiration with deep irony. Boxer’s “I will work harder” is not heroic — it is the response of someone who has been conditioned to accept exploitation as virtue. The harder he works, the more the pigs benefit, and the faster he is used up.

Clover, the maternal mare, watches Boxer with concern but cannot articulate her unease. She represents the animals who sense something is wrong but lack the education or confidence to speak up — another of Orwell’s critiques of how intellectual inequality enables oppression.

Orwell’s Message About Labour and Power

Through the windmill chapters, Orwell shows that the product of labour matters less than who controls it. The animals build the windmill, but the pigs decide what it is used for (eventually, grinding corn to sell for profit, not generating electricity for the animals). This mirrors how Soviet industrial output benefited the state apparatus, not the workers who produced it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Boxer is one of the most frequently examined characters. When writing about him, avoid simply describing him as “loyal and hardworking” — this is surface-level. Instead, analyse the irony of his slogans: “I will work harder” ensures his own destruction, and “Napoleon is always right” prevents him from ever seeing the truth. This ironic reading shows AO2 sophistication and links to Orwell’s AO3 warning about blind obedience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The windmill symbolises false progress — built on the animals’ suffering but benefiting only the pigs, mirroring Stalin’s Five-Year Plans.
  • Boxer’s blind loyalty and relentless work ethic make him the most exploited character — Orwell shows that unquestioning obedience enables tyranny.
  • Napoleon’s scapegoating of Snowball for the windmill’s collapse mirrors totalitarian propaganda that blames external enemies for internal failures.

lessons.title: The Purges & Terror
lessons.description: How Napoleon uses public executions and false confessions to terrorise the farm into submission.
lessons.content_html:
The Confessions and Executions (Chapter 7)

Chapter 7 is the darkest moment in Animal Farm. Napoleon orders all the animals to assemble in the yard, then calls forward four pigs who had previously questioned his decisions. With the dogs snarling beside him, Napoleon forces them to confess to being in secret contact with Snowball and plotting to sabotage the farm. The dogs immediately tear out their throats.

Then other animals step forward — hens, geese, a sheep — and confess to various crimes, all supposedly inspired by Snowball. Each confession is followed by execution. By the end, a pile of corpses lies at Napoleon’s feet, and the air is heavy with the smell of blood.

Key Fact

The purges directly mirror Stalin’s Great Purge (1936–1938), also known as the Great Terror. Stalin held show trials where former allies were forced to confess to impossible crimes before being executed. An estimated 750,000 people were killed during the Great Purge.

The Sixth Commandment — Rewritten

The Sixth Commandment originally read: “No animal shall kill any other animal.” After the executions, the animals remember this rule and feel uneasy. When Clover asks Muriel to read the commandment from the barn wall, it now reads: “No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.” The two added words change the entire meaning.

Orwell uses the commandments as a structural device to track the corruption of Animalism. Each alteration marks a new betrayal:

“No animal shall sleep in a bed” becomes “No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets” — when the pigs move into the farmhouse.

“No animal shall drink alcohol” becomes “No animal shall drink alcohol to excess” — when Napoleon discovers whisky.

“No animal shall kill any other animal” becomes “No animal shall kill any other animal without cause” — after the purges.

The animals think they must have misremembered the original wording. Orwell shows how cognitive dissonance enables oppression — rather than accept that their leaders are lying, the animals doubt their own memories.

Clover’s Silent Despair

After the executions, Clover climbs the hill overlooking the farm. Orwell describes her looking out over the landscape that “ought to have been a scene of tranquillity.” She tries to marshal her thoughts but cannot find the words to express what she feels. She knows this is not what Old Major envisioned, but she cannot articulate why or how things went wrong.

Key Fact

Clover’s scene on the hillside is one of the most poignant in the novella. Orwell deliberately denies her the ability to speak — she “would have protested if she could have found the right words.” This represents how ordinary people can sense injustice but, without education and political language, cannot challenge it. The absence of words is itself Orwell’s point about the power of language.

The confessions are one of the most disturbing aspects of the novella. Some animals may genuinely believe they have done wrong, having internalised the propaganda. Others may confess out of terror — they have watched others torn apart by the dogs and know resistance is futile.

Orwell leaves this ambiguous, mirroring the genuine uncertainty about why people confessed during Stalin’s show trials. Historians debate whether victims were tortured, threatened, ideologically broken, or simply desperate. Orwell captures all of these possibilities.

The hens who confess had previously staged a small rebellion, refusing to hand over their eggs for trade. Napoleon starved them into submission. Their “crime” was resisting an unjust order — but under Napoleon’s regime, any dissent is punishable by death.

The Banning of “Beasts of England”

After the purges, Napoleon bans “Beasts of England.” Squealer explains that the song is no longer necessary because the Rebellion is complete and the better society it promised has been achieved. A new anthem praising Napoleon replaces it. This is deeply ironic — the song represented hope for liberation, and its removal signals that hope’s death. The revolution has consumed its own ideals.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The purges mirror Stalin’s Great Terror — forced confessions and public executions used to eliminate dissent and create fear.
  • The commandments are rewritten to justify the pigs’ actions — each change marks a new stage in the corruption of Animalism.
  • Clover’s inability to articulate her despair represents how the absence of political language prevents resistance.

lessons.title: Napoleon's Cult of Personality
lessons.description: How Napoleon creates a god-like image through titles, ceremonies, and the rewriting of history.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Cult of Personality?

A cult of personality is when a leader uses propaganda to create a god-like public image. Stalin was a master of this — portraits, statues, and songs praised him as the “Father of Nations,” and cities were renamed in his honour. In Animal Farm, Napoleon develops his own cult of personality as the novella progresses.

Key Fact

Napoleon is given titles such as “our Leader, Comrade Napoleon,” “Father of All Animals,” “Terror of Mankind,” “Protector of the Sheep-fold,” and “Ducklings’ Friend.” These increasingly absurd titles mirror the grandiose titles given to Stalin and other dictators.

Squealer attributes all good fortune to Napoleon personally — every successful harvest, every egg laid, every drink of water is credited to “the leadership of Comrade Napoleon.” A poem by Minimus, the poet pig, is inscribed on the barn wall alongside a portrait of Napoleon, placed at the opposite end of the barn from the Seven Commandments.

Napoleon’s Growing Power and Privilege

As Napoleon’s cult grows, so do his privileges. The pigs move into the farmhouse, sleep in beds, eat at the dining table, and drink whisky. Napoleon rarely appears in public — when he does, he is surrounded by dogs and announced with a ceremonial cockerel crow. He eats from Jones’s own china and always enters from a different door to the other pigs.

Stalin lived in luxury in the Kremlin while millions of Soviet citizens starved. He had portraits in every public building, his name in every newspaper, and his birthday was a national holiday. Cities like Stalingrad were named after him.

Napoleon’s behaviour mirrors this precisely. He lives in comfort while the animals’ rations are repeatedly cut. His portrait replaces the commandments. His birthday is celebrated with a gun salute. Every success is attributed to him; every failure is blamed on Snowball.

Orwell highlights the irony that a revolution fought to end one form of tyranny (Jones/the Tsar) has simply replaced it with another. The pigs have not created equality — they have become the new ruling class.

Trade with Humans — Another Betrayal

Napoleon begins trading with neighbouring farms through a human broker named Mr Whymper. This directly contradicts the original principles of Animalism, which forbade all contact with humans. When the animals protest, Squealer insists that no such rule ever existed — it was a “lie” spread by Snowball.

Key Fact

The trading with humans represents the Soviet Union’s economic deals with Western capitalist nations. Despite communist ideology opposing capitalism, Stalin engaged in trade agreements when it suited him. Orwell uses this to show that ideological purity is always sacrificed when it conflicts with the ruling class’s interests.

The two neighbouring farmers represent rival political systems. Mr Frederick (Pinchfield Farm) represents Adolf Hitler and Nazi Germany — his farm is small, well-run, and he drives hard bargains. Mr Pilkington (Foxwood Farm) represents the Western capitalist powers, particularly Britain — his farm is larger but neglected.

Napoleon alternates between alliances with each, just as Stalin switched between hostility and cooperation with Germany and the West. The deal with Frederick (who pays with forged banknotes and later attacks the farm) mirrors the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 1939, which Stalin trusted before Hitler’s betrayal in 1941.

The Battle of the Windmill — when Frederick’s men attack and blow up the rebuilt windmill — represents Hitler’s invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa). The animals win but at enormous cost, just as Russia defeated Germany but suffered 27 million casualties.

Orwell’s Point About Power and Corruption

By Chapter 8, the novella’s central argument is clear: power inevitably corrupts. Napoleon has become indistinguishable from the human oppressors the revolution was supposed to replace. The commandments have been rewritten, the original ideals abandoned, and the working animals are worse off than ever. Orwell suggests this is not unique to the Russian Revolution — it is a pattern that recurs whenever a small group seizes power without accountability.
lessons.exam_tip_html: If asked about Napoleon, structure your answer chronologically to show his progression from silent schemer to absolute dictator. This demonstrates understanding of the novella’s structure (AO2) and allows you to draw specific historical parallels (AO3) at each stage. The best answers will note that Orwell never gives Napoleon a sympathetic moment — unlike Snowball or Boxer, he has no redeeming qualities, making him a purely allegorical figure.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Napoleon develops a cult of personality through titles, ceremonies, portraits, and Squealer’s propaganda — mirroring Stalin’s self-glorification.
  • Trade with humans and the alliance with Frederick show how revolutionary ideals are abandoned when they conflict with the ruling class’s interests.
  • By Chapter 8, Napoleon has become indistinguishable from the human tyrants the revolution was meant to overthrow — reinforcing Orwell’s cyclical structure.

lessons.title: The Death of Boxer & Betrayal
lessons.description: How Boxer's fate represents the ultimate betrayal of the working class and Orwell's most emotional moment.
lessons.content_html:
Boxer’s Collapse

Boxer has worked himself to exhaustion rebuilding the windmill for the second time. He is now twelve years old — past the retirement age he was promised under Animalism. One day, while hauling stone, his lungs give out and he collapses. He cannot get up. The other animals are horrified, especially Clover, who has watched Boxer’s decline with growing concern.

Boxer is philosophical about his injury. He says he had hoped to see the windmill finished before his retirement. He looks forward to spending his remaining years in the pasture that Old Major had promised all retiring animals would enjoy. The reader, of course, already senses that this promise will be broken.

Key Fact

Boxer was promised retirement at the age of twelve — a pension for loyal service. This promise represents the social contract between workers and the state: work hard, and you will be looked after. Napoleon’s betrayal of this promise is Orwell’s most damning indictment of the Soviet system.

The Knacker’s Van

Napoleon announces that Boxer will be sent to a veterinary hospital in Willingdon. A van arrives to collect him. But Benjamin, the cynical donkey who can read, notices the writing on the side: “Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler.” For the first time in the novella, Benjamin breaks his silence and screams for the animals to stop the van.

Clover cries out: “Boxer! Boxer! Boxer! Get out! Get out quickly! They’re taking you to your death!” Boxer tries to kick his way out of the van, but his strength has gone. The van drives away while the animals chase it helplessly.

This is the emotional climax of Animal Farm. Orwell strips away all allegory and political symbolism — what the reader experiences is raw grief and injustice. The most loyal, hardworking creature on the farm is sold to a knacker for profit.

Squealer later claims Boxer died peacefully at the hospital, with the words “Long live Comrade Napoleon” on his lips. He explains that the van had previously belonged to a knacker but was now owned by a vet who hadn’t repainted it. The animals, exhausted and defeated, accept this obvious lie.

Key Fact

Orwell reveals that Napoleon used the money from selling Boxer to the knacker to buy a case of whisky. This detail is the novella’s most savage moment of irony — a lifetime of loyal service literally converted into alcohol for the pigs.

Benjamin’s Silence and Its Meaning

Benjamin is the only animal besides the pigs who can read fluently, and the only one who has never been fooled by Squealer’s propaganda. His consistent refusal to act — his belief that “life would go on as it had always gone on — that is, badly” — makes him a deeply ambiguous figure.

Benjamin only acts when it is too late to save Boxer. Orwell seems to suggest that his silence throughout the novella makes him complicit in the pigs’ crimes. He has the intelligence to understand what is happening and the literacy to prove the commandments are being changed, but he does nothing.

Orwell uses Benjamin to criticise fatalism — the intellectual’s temptation to shrug and say “it was always going to happen.” By refusing to engage, Benjamin allows the pigs to act without challenge. His guilt is different from Boxer’s — Boxer is too trusting, but Benjamin is too cynical.

Together, Boxer and Benjamin represent two failures of the ordinary citizen: blind loyalty and passive cynicism. Orwell suggests that both enable tyranny, and that the only defence against dictatorship is informed, active engagement.

Orwell’s Emotional Impact

Boxer’s death is designed to make readers feel genuine anger. Orwell has spent the entire novella building sympathy for Boxer — his loyalty, his gentleness, his simple decency — only to show that these qualities are rewarded with betrayal. The emotional impact forces readers to engage with the political argument: if this makes you angry, Orwell implies, then you should be angry about what happened to the Soviet working class under Stalin.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Boxer’s death is the most emotionally powerful moment in the text. When writing about it, use precise quotations (“Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler”) and focus on Orwell’s structural choice to place this scene near the end of the novella. By this point, readers have seen every other betrayal — Boxer’s death is the culmination, not just an event. Linking this structural awareness to your analysis earns top AO2 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Boxer is sold to the knacker — his lifetime of loyalty is literally converted into whisky for the pigs, representing the ultimate betrayal of the working class.
  • Benjamin’s silence throughout the novella makes him complicit — Orwell criticises both blind loyalty (Boxer) and cynical passivity (Benjamin).
  • Boxer’s death is the emotional climax, designed to convert sympathy into political anger at the system that allowed it.

lessons.title: The Ending & the Moral
lessons.description: How the final scene delivers Orwell's devastating message and what the novella's cyclical structure means.
lessons.content_html:
The Pigs Walk on Two Legs

In the final chapter, the pigs complete their transformation into the very creatures they overthrew. One morning, Clover neighs in alarm and the animals rush outside to see the pigs walking upright on their hind legs. Squealer walks on two legs. Napoleon emerges last, carrying a whip in his trotter. The sheep, retrained by Squealer, now bleat: “Four legs good, two legs better!”

Key Fact

The transformation from “Four legs good, two legs bad” to “Four legs good, two legs better” is the novella’s single most powerful moment of political irony. The slogan that once defined the revolution is reversed to serve the new oppressors. Orwell shows that language itself can be weaponised to mean the exact opposite of its original intent.

The Seven Commandments have been erased entirely. In their place, a single commandment is painted on the barn wall: “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.” This paradox encapsulates Orwell’s entire argument about how language is corrupted to justify inequality.

The Final Scene — Pigs and Humans

The novella ends with a dinner party in the farmhouse. Napoleon hosts a group of human farmers, including Mr Pilkington. They sit at the table, drink together, and congratulate each other. Pilkington praises Napoleon for running a farm where the animals do more work and eat less food than any other farm in the county.

Napoleon announces that Animal Farm will be renamed “Manor Farm” — its original name under Jones. Even the farm’s identity has been erased. The name change symbolises the cyclical structure of the novella — everything has returned to how it was before the revolution.

During a game of cards, Napoleon and Pilkington both play an ace of spades simultaneously and accuse each other of cheating. A quarrel breaks out. The watching animals look from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again — “but already it was impossible to say which was which.”

This final sentence is one of the most famous in English literature. Orwell delivers his thesis in a single image: the revolutionaries have become indistinguishable from the oppressors they replaced. The card game quarrel suggests that powerful figures, regardless of ideology, will always cheat and fight for dominance.

The Cyclical Structure

Orwell deliberately structures the novella as a circle. The farm begins under human tyranny, passes through a brief period of hope, and returns to tyranny — only this time, the tyrants are pigs. This cyclical narrative implies that revolutions are doomed to repeat the patterns they aimed to break, unless the underlying power structures are fundamentally changed.

Key Fact

The renaming of Animal Farm back to “Manor Farm” completes the cycle. The name “Animal Farm” represented the revolution’s promise of a new beginning. Its erasure means the revolution has been entirely undone — not by external enemies, but by the very animals who led it.

Orwell’s message is layered and can be read at several levels:

Political: The Russian Revolution was betrayed by Stalin, who replaced one form of tyranny with another. This is a specific critique of Stalinism, not of socialism itself.

Universal: Power corrupts. Any revolution that concentrates power in a small elite without democratic accountability will produce new oppressors. The cycle of tyranny, revolution, and new tyranny is a pattern throughout history.

About language: Those who control language control thought. Propaganda, censorship, and the rewriting of history are the tools that enable oppression. Orwell believed that defending the integrity of language was a political act.

About responsibility: The animals’ failure to resist — whether through blind loyalty (Boxer), cynical passivity (Benjamin), or inability to think critically (the sheep) — makes them complicit. Orwell suggests that ordinary people have a duty to stay informed and hold their leaders accountable.

Why the Ending Matters for the Exam

The final scene is one of the most commonly examined passages. It works as a powerful conclusion to almost any essay question because it brings together all the novella’s major themes: power, corruption, propaganda, class, and the failure of revolution. Being able to analyse this scene in detail — with specific quotations and confident contextual links — will strengthen any response.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The final line (“it was impossible to say which was which”) should appear in almost every essay you write on Animal Farm. It is the novella’s thesis statement. When quoting it, analyse the structure (why Orwell places it last), the language (the repetition of “pig to man, man to pig”), and the context (Stalin’s embrace of the same power structures as the Tsars). This single quotation can earn marks across all three Assessment Objectives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The pigs become indistinguishable from humans — the revolution has produced the very tyranny it was meant to destroy.
  • The cyclical structure (Manor Farm → Animal Farm → Manor Farm) suggests that revolutions without democratic accountability are doomed to fail.
  • “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” is Orwell’s devastating summary of how language is corrupted to justify inequality.

AO2 (12): Language analysis — the corruption of the original commandment, the paradox as a rhetorical device. AO3 (6): Soviet inequality, the nomenklatura, the gap between communist ideals and Stalinist reality.

practice_questions.text: 'Animal Farm ends without hope.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: AO1 (12): Argue for (cyclical structure, total corruption, animals' helplessness) and against (the reader's anger is itself hope — Orwell writes to provoke change). AO2 (12): Analyse the ending's tone, the fable's moral function. AO3 (6): Orwell as a democratic socialist — he opposed Stalinism but believed in human potential. spelling/grammar: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the novella's structure to develop his argument about the corruption of power?
practice_questions.marks: AO1 (12): Track the structural arc from hope to despair. AO2 (12): Cyclical structure, the commandments as structural markers, the progressive erosion of democratic elements. AO3 (6): The trajectory of the Russian Revolution from 1917 to the 1940s.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell present the theme of class in Animal Farm?
practice_questions.marks: AO1 (12): Analyse the new class hierarchy — pigs, dogs, other animals. AO2 (12): How Orwell presents each class through characterisation and language. AO3 (6): Marxist class analysis, the irony of a classless revolution creating new classes.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use the pigs' transformation to humans to deliver the novella's moral?
practice_questions.marks: AO1 (12): Analyse the progression — walking upright, carrying whips, wearing clothes, dining with humans. AO2 (12): Symbolic transformation, the final image as climax. AO3 (6): Stalin's adoption of Tsarist privileges, the cyclical nature of oppression.

glossary_terms.definition: A statement that contradicts itself, often revealing a deeper truth or absurdity.
A narrative structure where the story ends in a similar position to where it began, suggesting repetition and inevitability.
A recurring sequence of events that returns to its starting point, suggesting that history repeats itself.
The political ideology and practices associated with Joseph Stalin, characterised by centralised authority, political repression, and a cult of personality.
